parts.title: Opening a bank account
parts.context: A customer phones a bank to open a current account.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Part 1. You will hear a customer phoning a bank to ask about opening an account. First, you have some time to look at questions 1 to 5.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: You will see that there is an example that has been done for you. On this occasion only, the conversation relating to this will be played first.

script.speaker: helen
script.text: Harbour Bank, Helen speaking. How can I help?

script.speaker: leo
script.text: Hello. I've just started a new job in the city, and I'd like to open a current account, please.

script.speaker: helen
script.text: Of course. I'll take your details first, and then I'll explain our accounts.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: The caller wants a current account, so 'current' has been written in the space. Now we shall begin. You should answer the questions as you listen, because you will not hear the recording a second time. Listen carefully and answer questions 1 to 5.

script.speaker: helen
script.text: Can I have your full name?

script.speaker: leo
script.text: Leo Marchetti. That's M-A-R-C-H-E-T-T-I.

script.speaker: helen
script.text: Thank you, Mr Marchetti. And your date of birth?

script.speaker: leo
script.text: The fourteenth of March, nineteen ninety-six.

script.speaker: helen
script.text: And your address?

script.speaker: leo
script.text: It's twelve Wellington Street. I only moved in last month.

script.speaker: helen
script.text: Do you have a recent bill as proof of address? It must be from the last three months.

script.speaker: leo
script.text: I have an electricity bill in my name. Would that be all right?

script.speaker: helen
script.text: That's perfect. A bank statement would also be fine, but I'm afraid a mobile phone bill wouldn't. And what is your occupation?

script.speaker: leo
script.text: I'm an engineer. I work for a company that builds bridges.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Before you hear the rest of the conversation, you have some time to look at questions 6 to 10.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Now listen and answer questions 6 to 10.

script.speaker: helen
script.text: Now, our accounts. We have three. The Basic account has no monthly fee. You get a debit card and online banking, but no overdraft.

script.speaker: leo
script.text: And the others?

script.speaker: helen
script.text: The Classic account is six pounds a month. As well as the debit card, you get mobile phone insurance, which covers theft and accidental damage.

script.speaker: leo
script.text: That sounds useful. What about the Premium account?

script.speaker: helen
script.text: That's fourteen pounds a month. It includes travel insurance and free access to airport lounges, which is popular with people who travel for work.

script.speaker: leo
script.text: I travel quite a lot, but only in this country.

script.speaker: helen
script.text: Then Classic is probably better value, as you won't need the travel insurance.

script.speaker: leo
script.text: I think so too. Can I open it online?

script.speaker: helen
script.text: Yes, or you can come to a branch with your passport. Either way it takes about fifteen minutes.

script.speaker: leo
script.text: Great. I'll do it online tonight. Thanks for your help.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: That is the end of Part 1. You now have half a minute to check your answers.

parts.title: A community radio station
parts.context: The manager of a radio station talks to a visiting group about its history and volunteers.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Part 2. You will hear the manager of a community radio station talking to a visiting group. First, you have some time to look at questions 11 to 15.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions 11 to 15.

script.speaker: maria
script.text: Hello, everyone, and welcome to Harbour FM. I'm Maria Costa, the station manager. I'd like to tell you a little about us before we start the tour.

script.speaker: maria
script.text: We started broadcasting in two thousand and nine. Some people think it was earlier, because the idea was first discussed in two thousand and five, but it took four years to get a licence.

script.speaker: maria
script.text: Our first studio was in a former shop on Quay Street. We had no money, so a local church lent us a hall for training, but all the broadcasting was done from the shop.

script.speaker: maria
script.text: Today we have about eighty volunteers and only three paid staff. At one time we had a hundred and twenty, but many were students who left when they graduated.

script.speaker: maria
script.text: Our most popular programme isn't the morning news, as you might expect. It's the Saturday sports phone-in, where listeners ring up to argue about the local football team.

script.speaker: maria
script.text: We're funded mostly by local businesses, which pay for advertising. We did apply for a government grant, but we were turned down, and we only get a few small donations from listeners.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Before you hear the rest of the talk, you have some time to look at questions 16 to 20.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Now listen and answer questions 16 to 20.

script.speaker: maria
script.text: If you'd like to volunteer, we ask a few things. First, everyone attends a training day, held on the first Saturday of every month. You'll learn to use the equipment, and what you can and cannot say on air. You also need to sign a volunteer agreement, which is a simple contract.

script.speaker: maria
script.text: You don't need a voice test, because we think anyone can learn, and we'll lend you headphones, so there's no need to buy your own. Nobody is expected to work night shifts, either.

script.speaker: maria
script.text: Next year, the big plan is to launch a podcast, so that people who miss a programme can listen to it again. We'd like a second studio too, but that's too expensive for now, and we have no plans to change our name.

script.speaker: maria
script.text: On today's visit, you'll be able to watch a live broadcast through the glass wall of the main studio, but please stay quiet, and don't knock on the glass. In the training studio, one of our volunteers will let you try the equipment.

script.speaker: maria
script.text: If you'd like to apply after today, send an email to the volunteer coordinator. Please don't phone, because the office is empty during the day. Now, if you'd follow me, and keep your voices low.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: That is the end of Part 2. You now have half a minute to check your answers.

parts.title: A study on procrastination
parts.context: Two psychology students plan how to write up their study on procrastination.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Part 3. You will hear two psychology students, Hana and Marcus, discussing a study on procrastination. First, you have some time to look at questions 21 to 25.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions 21 to 25.

script.speaker: hana
script.text: Marcus, I've been looking at the data for our procrastination study. Before we write it up, let's agree how we describe the sample.

script.speaker: marcus
script.text: We started with a hundred and fifty students, but twenty-two dropped out, didn't they?

script.speaker: hana
script.text: Yes, so we have a hundred and twenty-eight who completed everything.

script.speaker: marcus
script.text: Why did so many drop out? Was it the diary?

script.speaker: hana
script.text: Mostly. Keeping a daily diary for four weeks was too much for some of them. A couple said they simply forgot.

script.speaker: marcus
script.text: What was the biggest surprise in the results?

script.speaker: hana
script.text: I expected the students with the most work to procrastinate most, but it was the opposite. Those with a heavy workload were actually more organised.

script.speaker: marcus
script.text: Interesting. And the deadline effect? I remember that people did most of their work at the end.

script.speaker: hana
script.text: Yes, about seventy percent of the work was done in the final forty-eight hours, however long the assignment was.

script.speaker: marcus
script.text: Our tutor will want a recommendation. Should we suggest that universities set earlier deadlines?

script.speaker: hana
script.text: I'd be careful, because we didn't test that. A better suggestion is to ask lecturers to split large assignments into stages, with a short deadline for each stage.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Before you hear the rest of the discussion, you have some time to look at questions 26 to 30.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Now listen and answer questions 26 to 30.

script.speaker: hana
script.text: Now the method section. Let's describe it step by step. First, everyone completed a questionnaire about their study habits.

script.speaker: marcus
script.text: Then they kept the diary for four weeks, writing down each day what they worked on and for how long.

script.speaker: hana
script.text: And we collected the log data from the university's online platform, which recorded when they opened their course materials.

script.speaker: marcus
script.text: Don't forget that half of the group received weekly reminders by text message, and the other half didn't.

script.speaker: hana
script.text: Right. The reminders made no real difference, which is another finding. Finally, we interviewed twelve students, to ask them about the reasons for their choices.

script.speaker: marcus
script.text: That's the part I enjoyed most. Some of the explanations were really honest.

script.speaker: hana
script.text: We didn't offer any reward for taking part, so we were lucky that so many people did. Shall I write the first draft of the method?

script.speaker: marcus
script.text: Please. I'll start on the results.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: That is the end of Part 3. You now have half a minute to check your answers.

parts.title: Lecture: the invention of photography
parts.context: A history lecture on the people who invented photography.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Part 4. You will hear a lecture about the invention of photography. First, you have some time to look at questions 31 to 40.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions 31 to 40.

script.speaker: lecturer
script.text: Good morning. Today I want to look at the invention of photography, which was not the work of one person, but of several people working in different countries.

script.speaker: lecturer
script.text: The starting point was the camera obscura, a darkened room or box with a small hole in one wall. Light from outside passes through the hole and projects an upside-down picture of the scene on the opposite wall. Artists had used it for centuries to help them draw.

script.speaker: lecturer
script.text: The problem was how to make the picture permanent. In the eighteen twenties, a French inventor named Nicéphore Niépce coated a metal plate with a light-sensitive substance called bitumen, and placed it in a camera obscura at an upstairs window. After an exposure of about eight hours, he had the oldest surviving photograph, a view of rooftops and a courtyard.

script.speaker: lecturer
script.text: Niépce later worked with Louis Daguerre, who discovered that a plate coated with silver, and treated with the vapour of mercury, produced a much clearer image in only a few minutes. The process was announced in eighteen thirty-nine. But each daguerreotype was unique, and it could not be copied.

script.speaker: lecturer
script.text: Meanwhile, in England, William Henry Fox Talbot developed a process using paper to make a negative, from which any number of positive prints could be made. That is the principle on which film photography was based until the digital age.

script.speaker: lecturer
script.text: Photography became widespread only when George Eastman introduced the Kodak camera in eighteen eighty-eight. It was loaded with a roll of film, and his slogan was, you press the button, we do the rest. Customers sent the whole camera back to the factory, where the film was developed and the camera was reloaded.

script.speaker: lecturer
script.text: The effects were far-reaching. Before photography, only wealthy people could afford a painted portrait. Now ordinary families could have a picture of themselves, and newspapers and scientists could record events and discoveries accurately. Next week we'll look at early cinema.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: That is the end of Part 4. You now have half a minute to check your answers.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: That is the end of the Listening test.
